After the F1 race in Vegas, we went to a party at XS nightclub at Encore. The Chainsmokers performed. 

I struck up a conversation with a guy visiting from NYC. Very successful finance guy. Looks wise, he was a 5 but his wife is a S tier 9 (she was there also). We ended up talking about lot of random stuff including dating/relationships. 

He made a few points that were interesting:

1) He believes that looksmaxxing is mostly correct but that for men, past a certain looks threshold, it doesn't matter that much in getting girls. 

2) I asked him about genuine attraction and whether it bothers him that there's such a big looks gap between him and his wife. He said that attraction for women is more nuanced than what Red Pill says: mainly that attraction is highly contextual & volatile. A woman can go from intense attraction to zero instantly for whatever reason. 

3) He admitted that if he were broke, his wife would not have married him but he wasn't bothered by that. He pointed out that if she weren't hot he wouldn't have married her so ultimately both parties got what they wanted. I asked him about concerns over cheating and he said that if a woman wants to cheat, she will do so, regardless of how attractive she is. And the guy can't do anything about it. Given that marriage is risky to begin with, he said you might as well marry the hottest girl you can. 

4) He said the benefits of being with a stunning woman is way more than just sex. His professional & social standing have skyrocketed: he gets instant respect & credibility from men and women alike. Most importantly, he said being with her has helped alleviate prior insecurities about his looks and he finally feels at peace with himself. If he had married a 5, he told me he would have struggled with constant insecurities and would have tried to cheat. 

I am not saying I agree with all of his points but it was interesting to hear his takes.

Active asset managers aggressively rotated out of stocks last week:

The NAAIM Exposure Index is down to 51 points, its lowest since April 2025.

This measures the average exposure to US equities reported by members of the National Association of Active Investment Managers.

The index has dropped -36 points, or -41%, over the last 2 weeks, marking its largest 2-week decline since November 2023.

This brings the 4-week average of this metric down to 71 points, its lowest since March 2026.

For perspective, the index bottomed at 13 points during the 2022 bear market and 11 points during the 2020 pandemic. 

Last week's sentiment flip spanned from retail to institutions.

a16z's Justine Moore and Olivia Moore partnered with The Prompting Company to test four consumer agents across 1,270 prompts and 11,307 completed runs.

Specific customer needs can overturn an agent's default recommendation. Shipping, returns, and seller credibility influence its choice. Requiring an account can stop it before checkout.

For businesses, winning an agent's business means making your product's value clear and giving the agent a path to actually buy or use it.

Full piece from a16z's Justine Moore and Olivia Moore: https://www.a16z.news/p/welcome-to-the-b2a-economy-how-agents

OpenAI's Joy Jiao on building a Codex for scientists:

"One of the biggest things that we see with the models today is that there's what we call a capability overhang, and this means that there's a lot of things the models can do, but no one knows about it, and so no one has access to that."

"What we really wanna do is bring something that is as good as Codex for coders, for scientists and to biotechs and pharma."

"When we are training GPT-Rosalind, we have all these interesting capabilities in the model in both chemistry and structural biology. We see that the models are doing really well on the benchmarks."

"But one repeated theme we've seen is that people don't know how to use the models. They don't know even what prompts to use, what questions to ask. And I think this is really where you need an exceptionally good product or a good harness around the model to really make that capability accessible to people."

@joyjiao12

Exa predicts that by 2030, AI agents will search the web 1,000x more than people do.

Harvard roommates Will Bryk and Jeff Wang started the company in 2021 to build a better search engine. Two weeks after Exa launched, ChatGPT came out.

Agents are a new kind of searcher, and Exa is built for them.

The company has grown 10x for three consecutive years, now handles 2 billion requests a month, and raised at a $2.2B valuation earlier this year.

Will and Jeff named it Exa after 10¹⁸, a smaller number than the googol (10¹⁰⁰) that inspired Google's name. Their explanation: "less is more."

I am astronomically happy as an NVIDIA employee

Ive used NVIDIA products my entire life and as a kid I counted down the days to every graphics card launch (this pic is from me as a chud at 14)

at 14 I went to the 1080 launch event and saw jensen on stage for the first time and in that moment I knew I had to become an engineer and work for jensen and this mission

first it was gaming then it was NVIDIA's cuda accelerated libraries which gave me an edge over my machine learning peers in college and now Im serving llms on the SAME hardware

all my life Ive worked my hardest to be part of this culture this company and this mission, I was devastated when JHH got ousted, few months after I got in full time

during the NVIDIA internship I knew I had to stay, I took 18 hours of machine learning courses in another city then drove to the office for a full 8 hour workday and I did both, social life and mental were sacrificed, no regrets, I am so happy I did that.

I was worried I wouldnt get the offer if I left so I kept fighting for extensions until my internship lasted a full year, I was hired on graduation this May

I sacrificed everything because I needed to be here

Im so proud to call Jensen my ceo and leader

thread_tweets.text:
1. Seed funding is becoming more concentrated

In 2026, 13 startups raised $100M+ at seed, matching the 2021 record.

But the median seed round was just $2.8M.

AI labs need big research budgets. Though I wouldn't confuse those giant rounds with what most founders can raise. https://t.co/4dJDV3xNGx

thread_tweets.text:
2. First-time founders have some serious competition

34% of seed founders in 2026 had started another company before. In 2021, it was 24%.

thread_tweets.text:
3. Series A funding has increased significantly

thread_tweets.text:
I heavily disagree with your other comment when you say Jensen doesn't solve anything. 

Jensen doesn't change macro issues with interest rates, credit/cash tightening (aside from maybe supplier financing). 

But he does cause accelerated upstream capacity procurement patterns, (which gives more durability visibility + more upstream capex commitments). 

Same thing with greater confidence in $NVDA's ecosystem like Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN. 

People argue downside reflexivity today:
-> valuations crash
-> less willingness to support vendor financing/guarantees. 
-> outflow to other ecosystems like TPUs + $AMD (Nvidia ecosystem push decline further eg. CPO), and so on. 
-> cycle of suck

Then there's other concurrent issues like the $500B AI financing with insurance + residual guarantees that was in trouble with Jensen gone. 

But same can be applied the other way upstream again with valuations + confidence + financing with Jensen's return. 

This is different from saying there's going to be a cash crunch and aggregate AI capex will keep exponentially increasing, my point is very narrow. 

But I'd argue Jensen alone does meaningfully increase upstream AI capex spend than when he's gone.

From Everpure earnings, AI capex is broadening to small business and random parts of the market (eg. insurance companies) because economics make sense. 

Not just handful of big buyers. 

People like to say capacity glut but B300 rates haven't really materially gone down, It went from $7.56 -> $7.65 -> $7.47 (compute glut timeframe)-> then up again $7.58 over past few weeks... 

$CRWV also says 10x qualified demand > supply for 2027, so there's too much demand. I wouldn't extrapolate several troubled Neoclouds in Asia to the entire compute market. 

As for past that, who knows, maybe there will be re-acceleration with other sources of demand. AI is crazy and keeps evolving every month.

tweets.text:
Ooo found $SMTC laser disclosures in earnings interesting after their HieFo acquisition: 

- UHP 400mW lasers under development (further behind $AAOI in this aspect since AOI has been doing quals).

In terms of laser revenue: 
-  3-4x capacity expansion EOY, another 3-4x end of next year. 
-> $25M/quarter EOY after 3x
-> ~$$100M quarter after 4x

- NPO engagement with 4 US hyperscalers and 3 Chinese hyperscalers (Aug 2027–Jan 2028 initial revenue for NPO for timelines)

- "developing CPO scale-up lasers, but that's a contribution of potential revenue beyond 2027" in terms of timeline

- "NPO represents a great near-term opportunity" relative to CPO

- "We wanted to catch the next wave, so that is a 3.2T" (from previous earnings)

It would be nice if $SIVE learned a thing or two about doing economic disclosures similar to this ($ scale of capacity, engagement scale. 

Semtech's strat is probably VHP/UHP lasers for NPO/CPO and 3.2T for pluggables since they missed the initial wave. 

Anyway, they look commercially behind compared to the rest (100-150mW only sampling now)... but very credible and interesting competitor emerging in 2028 + additional TAM expansion on top of TIA/Drivers.  

TLDR: HieFo acquisition might be goated (~$300m-$400m exit 2027 annualized capacity revenue opportunity, probably a lot more for 2028)... 

If it were standalone under Semtech I could see it being $1B-$2B+ just based on opportunity alone, but they got it for like ~$34M from US Gov forced divestiture.

Our SPY speculative flow indicator triggered a washout signal right before today's rally.

The reading fell to 20.5 on Friday and has not been this low since March 2020. The AI selloff had already drained speculative demand from the market, leaving stocks set up for a sharp rebound when Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang this morning.

Positioning washouts have not always marked the cycle bottom. In 2022, our indicator flagged bear market rallies of 11% and 17%. Both fully reversed because the Fed tightening behind that selloff never let up.

The current risk-off macro regime makes this more likely a bear market rally than the start of a sustained cyclical rebound.

thread_tweets.text:
Thanks for clarifying. I wouldn't put it past them. I do think American closed source models are aggressively trying to build fake regulatory moats, for lack of real economic moats against open weights. I agree.

Having worked for the FAA for 12 years, at one of the two key hubs that control most of the national system, there are 30-year old servers that if someone knocks something over, all planes nationwide have to land. Some classically bearded IT guy and his five colleagues are like the Avengers on that server room in a large building keeping nationwide planes going.

But by extension, if someone wants to control things, they have to go through that IT guy as well. Between high management and the direct systems, there's some bearded autist that isn't deep state, but is often a contractor. It would be kind of hard for higher-ups to just flip a button and shut things down without whistleblowers. I know enough to know that they have to go through some layers, some beards. Not impossible, but I can picture them and it's not some abstract government switch. Takes real work.

This theory competes with the related concept that a lot of old government and bank systems are part of the ongoing vulnerability where AI makes hacking cheaper and we're in a stage where everything has to use AI to harden. And what's not likely to be at the forefront of AI hardening? Government.

In other words, some things just get hacked because they haven't kept up.

My next sci fi book is about a psyop, btw. I get it.

Thanks for clarifying. I wouldn't put it past them. I do think American closed source models are aggressively trying to build fake regulatory moats, for lack of real economic moats against open weights. I agree.

Having worked for the FAA for 12 years, at one of the two key hubs that control most of the national system, there are 30-year old servers that if someone knocks something over, all planes nationwide have to land. Some classically bearded IT guy and his five colleagues are like the Avengers on that server room in a large building keeping nationwide planes going.

But by extension, if someone wants to control things, they have to go through that IT guy as well. Between high management and the direct systems, there's some bearded autist that isn't deep state, but is often a contractor. It would be kind of hard for higher-ups to just flip a button and shut things down without whistleblowers. I know enough to know that they have to go through some layers, some beards. Not impossible, but I can picture them and it's not some abstract government switch. Takes real work.

This theory competes with the related concept that a lot of old government and bank systems are part of the ongoing vulnerability where AI makes hacking cheaper and we're in a stage where everything has to use AI to harden. And what's not likely to be at the forefront of AI hardening? Government.

In other words, some things just get hacked because they haven't kept up.

My next sci fi book is about a psyop, btw. I get it.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
If I scrunched the math I probably made more per year with my old web2 digital marketing business than I have in crypto per year. 

But I don't regret jumping into crypto at all - not even 1%. 

My web2 business was basically meaningless - like the vast majority of economic stuff people do in today's world. 

It was convincing boomers to sign up for life insurance leads and mortgage refi leads and dating sites and etc - or convincing people on TikTok to buy random ecom gadgets (which is fine - but not overly fulfilling). 

Whereas with crypto I have had (an admittedly tiny) part of something that I genuinely think has great significance historically.  

Its easy to get cynical now, but crypto really is a massive advancement technologically, and something that is a clear net good for humanity.  And I still believe that- however slowly- it will absorb and replace the legacy tradfi system. 

Being in crypto full-time also feels 'real' and 'visceral' in a way that most things in the modern world do not. 

One of the biggest complaints about modernity is that "actions don't really have consequences". 

That it is like flag football or bowling with bumper pads or something, and not entirely 'real'. 

But crypto is VERY real, with VERY real stakes. 

Which is one reason I think people get so addicted to it.

In addition, by jumping into crypto full-time I've been able to be engage here on CT with the most intellectually brilliant people on the planet. 

I've made countless close friendships, I've been able to write a ton, and engage with other people's art and writing, and learn utterly insane amounts about economics, finance, history, government, human behavior, etc that I would not have had I stuck with digital marketing. 

But yeah... in short... I absolutely love crypto and love CT and I am incredibly grateful I dove into it when I did...

I mention this because I just thought it was really interesting on how big our investing world has gotten and not for the first time but interesting so. Space, meaning the universe above us, is now a consideration when it comes to loan covenants. I read over the weekend in the FT that “Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.”
“SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concern that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming the semiconductors for sale in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter. It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the final documents.”

thread_tweets.text:
Instead of calling for an end to the Iran War or any amount of fiscal discipline (deficit is now running at >$2 trillion), both of which would bring the inflation rate down, Bill Ackman is suggesting the Fed should simply raise their inflation target to 3% - essentially tolerating a further destruction in purchasing power.

We've already had 4% inflation for over 6 years and instead of hiking interest rates to attack this scourge the Fed should just throw their hands up and accept it? In doing so they would lose any remaining credibility that they have.

Who would raising the inflation target hurt the most? The lowest income workers whose wages would not keep pace with higher prices. They spend a higher portion of their salary on essential items like food and gasoline and have the lowest amount of financial assets.

Who would accepting higher inflation help the most? The highest income workers who spend a far lower percentage of their income on essential items and have the most invested in financial assets that benefit from currency debasement.

The stock market fell 10% in a month, then recovered almost half of that in a single day.

If you spend a moment reflecting on what just happened, you might have the biggest realization of your investing life: 𝗡𝗼𝗯𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴.

The market fell because it fell. Then it went up because it went up. None of this could have been consistently predicted.

Technical analysis, macro predictions, market narratives, valuation arguments. It’s all mumbo jumbo.

Sometimes the market loves expensive stocks, and valuations can remain extreme for years. Other times, even a forward P/E of 10 won’t save you.

The sooner you accept that you have no control over short-term market movements, the better investor you’ll become.

There is only one enduring truth: 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲. 𝗕𝘂𝘆 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿, 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲.

The formula below is not designed to identify the exact bottom, whether tomorrow, next month or three months from now. It’s a formula for building wealth over decades.

Share it with everyone you love. You don’t need to understand macroeconomics, technical analysis or market narratives to follow it.

In fact, the less you think you know about markets, the better this formula might work for you. Because you’ll be less tempted to interfere with it.

The stock market fell 10% in a month, then recovered almost half of that in a single day.

If you spend a moment reflecting on what just happened, you might have the biggest realization of your investing life: 𝗡𝗼𝗯𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴.

The market fell because it fell. Then it went up because it went up. None of this could have been consistently predicted.

Technical analysis, macro predictions, market narratives, valuation arguments. It’s all mumbo jumbo.

Sometimes the market loves expensive stocks, and valuations can remain extreme for years. Other times, even a forward P/E of 10 won’t save you.

The sooner you accept that you have no control over short-term market movements, the better investor you’ll become.

There is only one enduring truth: 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲. 𝗕𝘂𝘆 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝗿, 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗹𝘆, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲.

The formula below is not designed to identify the exact bottom, whether tomorrow, next month or three months from now. It’s a formula for building wealth over decades.

Share it with everyone you love. You don’t need to understand macroeconomics, technical analysis or market narratives to follow it.

Correlation does not imply causation.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
New High Conviction Buy: $INSM

Market Cap: $22.4B
Portfolio Allocation: 5%
Current Price: $103
Average Analyst Price Target: $215

Insmed ( $INSM ) is one of those rare situations where Wall Street seems to be focused on the next quarter, while some of the smartest biotech investors are looking several years ahead. We have seen similar pattern in all our recent wining picks.

The company develops medicines for serious lung diseases with few effective treatment options. Its lead product, Brinsupri, was recently launched for patients with bronchiectasis suffering from recurrent lung infections.

Earlier this year, the stock fell nearly 50% after the initial launch failed to meet the market’s extremely high expectations. Investors had expected an explosive rollout, but early prescription growth came in slower than hoped, leading many to question whether the launch was falling apart.

So far, that doesn’t appear to be the case.

Prescription trends have continued to improve, physicians remain optimistic, and several recent reports from JPMorgan, UBS and other research firms support our view that the market became overly focused on the first few months of prescriptions while missing the much bigger story. They also believe Brinsupri still has the potential to become a multi-billion-dollar drug as physician adoption expands and reimbursement improves over time.

From a technical standpoint, the stock also appears to have found a bottom after the 50% decline, with selling pressure easing while the underlying business continues to execute.

That alone would make Insmed interesting. But the pipeline may be even more valuable.

The company’s inhaled treprostinil program for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) could become another major growth driver, with important clinical data expected in 2026. If successful, Insmed would evolve from a one-product company into a diversified rare disease leader with multiple blockbuster opportunities.

Wall Street still sees substantial upside. Average analyst price targets remain well above today’s share price, with many analysts believing the recent selloff reflects timing rather than a deterioration in the long-term opportunity.

Perhaps the most interesting signal, however, comes from who owns the stock.

This isn’t a company being accumulated by generalist momentum funds. It is owned by some of the most respected healthcare investors in the world.

RTW Investments: 7.9% of its portfolio.
Baker Bros. Advisors: 7.0%.
Stanley Druckenmiller: 6.4%.
And perhaps most impressively, Darwin Global Management, one of biotech’s premier specialist hedge funds, has made Insmed roughly 68% of its disclosed public equity portfolio.

That level of concentration is almost unheard of. Specialist biotech investors spend years building relationships with physicians, researchers and management teams. While no investor is always right, seeing multiple world-class healthcare investors independently build such meaningful positions deserves attention.

The investment case ultimately comes down to one question.

If Brinsupri continues executing as prescription trends suggest, and the PAH program delivers positive clinical data next year, today’s valuation could look surprisingly inexpensive in hindsight.

The market is pricing execution risk.

The specialists appear to believe the market is underestimating the probability of success.

That’s exactly the kind of disconnect that often creates the best long-term investment opportunities.

Brokers research attached below.

No. Here’s what really happened.

Jensen started Nvidia in 1993, before the modern era of founder control and dual-class stock began with Google and Facebook.

Because he went public in the 1990s, he inherited all the 20th century overhead of endless public company paperwork, rather than staying private for as long as possible as is also now typical.

This is why Jensen had much less control than a modern founder/CEO. Like Jack Dorsey at Twitter, he got gradually boxed into a corner by the fact that he couldn’t raise huge amounts of capital outside his company to clear the board of cruft.

You see, as CEO, you report to the board. And you can’t do outside activities without their approval. So actions that would remove a board member that doesn’t want to step down are hard to take. Unless the CEO is also part of a shareholder majority, or has dual class / founder control, which Jensen didn’t in this case, as explained above…he can’t pick the board.

Like Bezos, though, Jensen is a workhorse and somehow made it all work despite that. Moreover, because Nvidia is a hardware company, and had a relatively low market cap until the AI boom, it didn’t attract notice from envious wokes until the last few years. 

Wokes don’t know or care about GPUs, but they do care about market caps, and the rise of AI, and especially open source AI, all of which is a threat to their power. Along with useful idiot “nationalists”, they began plotting to steal control of Jensen’s multi-trillion-dollar company from him.

In this plot, they were aided by a second angle of vulnerability. Jensen didn’t just have old board members he couldn’t remove. Due to DEI policies, he was also forced to bring new board members on, from demographics favored by the far left (eg, not veterans).

Conformist board members like this act like sleeper cells. They are often useless or inactive in peacetime scenarios. Then they activate in response to press or state pressure. In this case, they then got beaten back just as quickly by the reversal of the state’s position.

Anyway, Dorsey needed Elon to come in with his enormous new resources to sweep the board clean. Today, it’s quite possible that Jensen, as the survivor of this character assassination, will similarly figure out a way to fire this incompetent board and assert proper founder control — as is a best practice in the modern era.

tweets.text:
Founders produce higher returns than non-founders. This is an empirical fact.

So: business school curricula should be changed, and good governance should be redefined as founder control and dual-class stock. Shareholders are still protected by easy liquidation and their ability to fund new entrants. After all, you don’t invest in a company based on who’s on the board. That’s largely ceremonial.

The key difference from the 20th century is that it was prohibitively difficult in 1950 to found a manufacturing company, because assembly lines cost so much, the communists controlled much of the world, and even America had 90% marginal tax rates. It was the century of centralization, the individual powerless before the institution.

Today it is no longer prohibitively difficult to found a tech company, because software costs so little, much of the world has turned to free markets, and capital flows at the speed of the Internet. This is the century of decentralization, at least in the West, with the institution falling to the individual.

For example: Anthropic was started just a few years ago and is beating even Google at its own game. If we get many open weights models, their moat will also in turn erode.

So: all 20th century corporate governance was based on the idea that “the company is hard to replace, but its CEO isn’t.” The Harvard MBA is premised on the professional manager. It was expensive to start a new company with all the assembly lines, so make sure it doesn’t fail by making every employee replaceable. Managers were abundant so capital became the scarce asset.

By contrast, the entire 21st century model is based on the idea that “A tech founder is hard to replace, but the company isn’t.” The YCombinator model is premised on the startup founder. It is inexpensive to start a new company with a few lines of code, so make sure it doesn’t fail by having an irreplaceable team. Capital is abundant so founders become the scarce asset.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
All the business school curricula need to be rewritten for the 21st century.

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

However, all these intuitions and best practices, the conventions that built billion and trillion dollar companies, have only been informally advocated in blog posts and contracts. To change the defaults, we’ll need to actually write a new curriculum.

Jane, I’ve actually seen you be more reasonable than most in your profession. So here’s my attempt to reason with you.

Everyone isn’t the same. Founders produce higher returns than non-founders, just like math Olympiad winners outscore math amateurs. This is a numerical fact; see graph below.

However, everyone is the same as a journo. Thus, it is no longer a useful tactic to crop a tweet and post it out of context under the assumption your subject doesn’t see it, as it’ll be directly rebutted. Because citizens now have comparable distribution to corporate journalists. Thus, I quote the full tweet below, which briefly explains why the internet century is different than the centralized century.

Basically: the era of newspaper nepotist heirs is ending. And the era of self-made technologists like Jensen Huang is beginning.

So, come back to your libertarian and conservative roots; there’s still time to switch sides back to the free Internet.

tweets.text:
The term AI agents sounds cringe

Which makes sense because it's primarily used by people in polycules keeping their MacBook lids open

In reality it's quite simple

If you were to hire someone to work for you, and you gave them a task with no prior guidance or training, you wouldn't be too surprised if they produced shit

AI models are the same

To get useful work out, you need to put effort in to give models the appropriate context, tools, and instructions

A common complaint from people is "I don't even know what I would ask it/what I would use it for."

You don't need to know the answer beforehand. If you give the model enough information, it will be able to propose pretty intelligent things itself.

The simplest way to kick this off would be to create a folder on your desktop (literally an empty folder) and then open up the Claude desktop app or whatever you use and point it at that folder

The reason you're pointing the model at a folder is that it can read, write, code, and remember shit instead of just being a fancy Google search that forgets everything

If you want bonus points you can go into Settings > Connectors/Plugins and give it read access to places where you do your work or hobbies e.g. your email, calendar, Google Drive etc.

Then you can fire off something as simple as:

I'm setting up this folder because I want to do cool shit with LLMs. I'm a total noob. If I've connected anything like my email or calendar, have a look through them first (read-only, don't touch or send anything). Then grill me a question or two at a time about my work, goals, hobbies, and whatever is currently wasting my time or cool stuff I want to do. Once you develop a decent understanding of me and my goals etc., write it all down in a file in this folder so you remember it next time. Then tell me 5 genuinely useful things you could actually do for me (skip the boring 'summarise my emails' slop) and we'll start on the best one.

That's it. You've just used an AI agent - congrats

You are just weeks away from vibe coding a Bloomberg terminal and 3D printing a fleshlight

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Anthony, the "spy" story appears to be as fake as Russiagate. Here are the facts as I understand them.

(1) First, Alice Huang was at a company called Megaspeed[1], which everyone agrees bought Nvidia chips to sell to Southeast Asian companies called neoclouds. This is in itself completely legal under US law.

(2) However, some both inside and outside the admin didn't like this. They want to block Chinese nationals from accessing cloud services with Nvidia GPUs even if those servers are located outside China. Fine, but the so-called Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to block this has passed the House but not the Senate, and is not law[2].

(3) Singapore's government also looked into this when Alice Huang was on their soil[3] and didn't find any evidence that Megaspeed was actually selling chips to China illegally — let alone that she was a "Chinese spy." They did give her an entry ban, but that's like a visa denial.

(4) The related point is that it's not actually illegal to sell Nvidia chips to China! Since the Biden admin, there has been a complex and constantly-shifting set of export restrictions on chips. As of right now, Nvidia is allowed to sell H200s[4] to China, and indeed has designed these to comply with applicable law.

(5) But you know what...China actually also doesn't want Nvidia chips in China [5,6], because they want to build up their homegrown chip industry. The Nvidia chips are so good that China doesn't want to remain dependent on American chips, or vulnerable to possible US backdoors.

(6) The broader point is that this is an argument between nationalists and capitalists. Nationalists argue that US companies shouldn't even get close to selling to China, and shouldn't even be selling to neoclouds, even if it's "technically" legal. Capitalists argue that it's impossible for American companies to dominate world markets without, you know, being allowed to dominate world markets by actually competing in them. And that it's one thing to restrict physical sales to China, and quite another to require proof-of-citizenship for every single cloud access.

(7) Here's the thing: it doesn't make sense for one of the (few!) industries where America has a trade surplus with China to be summarily cut off, if you're worried about trade surpluses. It doesn't make sense to remove your number one AI CEO, if you want to be number one in AI. And it truly doesn't make sense to do to Jensen Huang what the communists did to Jack Ma[7], if your goal is fighting communism.

(8) So, to summarize: there's no proof of spying, as Blanche at DOJ has admitted[8], which rebuts your FBI/DOJ points. The Wachtell investigation you raise is just an in-house thing[9] ordered by the Nvidia board. And so all that's left is some affairs, which society has agreed is not disqualifying, given the realities of both Clinton and Trump.

In short: do you want a communist society like China, where Jack Ma's company can be stolen from him overnight on false pretenses? Or do you want some semblance of rule of law? If so, you should support the restoration of Jensen Huang to the company he built.

Citations follow in the next tweet.

The first practical solution to witness encryption for general NP:

https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2971

At 100 bits security: ciphertext size: <8 GB, encryption and decryption time: seconds. Formally lean verified from standard security assumptions (bi-linear generic group and random oracle model under Module-SIS.) 

This work is built on recent feasibility results by Hair and Sahai and improves their ciphertext size and encryption time by 10 orders of magnitude and decryption time by 6 orders.

Our motivation is non-interactive proof verification on Bitcoin without the need for challengers and operators, but witness encryption is a fundamental problem and we hope this work will open up many other use cases.

Many times when you don't know how cryptography works or how blockchains work, you'll think something like:

"I want to publish a password protected zip of the Epstein files on the Bitcoin blockchain, and then I want it decrypted 2 years into the future using a smart contract! Even if I die, it won't matter, because the smart contract will decrypt it for everyone!" 

Then smart people will tell you that that's impossible

The blockchain either knows something or it doesn't

It can't, in 2 years, magically know the password to the Epstein file .zip archive... UNLESS YOU HAVE WITNESS ENCRYPTION 

Witness encryption changes the whole game of what's possible to do on blockchains 

You can write essentially smart contracts that have conditions that your blockchain's programming language doesn't know how to write the code for 

This also *opens a path* to trustless L2s on Bitcoin (requires a setup ceremony and some other pieces)

You can make something like Shielded Bitcoin (Zcash-like payments with Bitcoin) without trusting a federation. Like BitVM but without the BitVM-part. 

It's like being a plumber or mechanic and someone just invented the screwdriver (or made screwdrivers "practical", whatever, same thing)

It's like being an electrician and someone just invented the multimeter 

It's ridiculous

The AI capex boom has created a surge in nonresidential construction jobs. 

The multiplier has spread to durable manufacturing production, payrolls, and beyond.

It is understandable that fear of a major AI slowdown (for projects in 2028+) could trigger an economic slowdown, but goods-sector payrolls are more leading, and the income earned from this boom today and over the next few quarters will not unwind immediately. 

The tightening in the labor market today will create some upward pressure on inflation. 

Stock prices are volatile as earnings growth in 2028+ is discounted today, but it's not quite the same with economic activity, growth, and inflation. 

The more near-term risk to the economy is housing, as it's the only sector with measurable, ongoing job losses and activity slowdowns in force today.

A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Jensen Huang is returning as CEO of Nvidia $NVDA, with the company announcing his immediate reinstatement as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the board following a unanimous vote by directors. The decision reverses the board's earlier opposition to his return and follows extensive discussions with Huang and senior U.S. government officials, after which directors concluded that his reinstatement would not pose a national security risk. Harvey Jones will remain board chairman, while Colette Kress will return to her CFO responsibilities after serving as interim CEO. Importantly, the independent investigation into Huang's conduct and the reported foreign intelligence effort remains ongoing, with Nvidia introducing additional compliance oversight and beginning a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Huang pledged his full cooperation and expressed excitement about returning to lead Nvidia during what he described as the beginning of a new industrial revolution. The announcement triggered an extraordinary reaction on Wall Street, with Nvidia reportedly adding approximately $980B in market capitalization in a single trading session, highlighting how heavily investors value Huang's leadership and his central role in the company's AI infrastructure strategy, product development, and long-term competitive positioning.

2. President Trump said his intervention was instrumental in securing Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia $NVDA CEO, claiming the process became significantly easier following the company's recent stock price decline. Trump acknowledged that stock market movements likely influenced his decision to intervene, revealing that he personally provided Nvidia's board with assurances regarding national security concerns and potential prosecution of Huang, telling directors that Huang was “absolutely fine.” Trump also disclosed that he spoke directly with Huang, who reportedly promised to work harder than ever, while emphasizing his confidence in the executive's leadership and technological expertise. Addressing concerns surrounding the broader AI industry, Trump said he is no longer worried about an AI bubble, highlighting Nvidia's development of next-generation chips far beyond Blackwell that he believes competitors will struggle to replicate. When questioned about allegations involving Alice Huang and potential Chinese intelligence connections, Trump downplayed the concerns, questioning how unusual contact with China really is. 

3. JPMorgan says Tesla $TSLA has strengthened its lead in consumer autonomous driving following the initial rollout of Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, describing the update as further evidence of Tesla's technological head start over competing automakers. The new software introduces a substantially redesigned AI driving architecture, including an upgraded vision system shared across FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus, improved navigation learned from real-world fleet data, and enhanced environmental perception. Tesla claims the update delivers approximately a 25x improvement in handling safety-critical driving scenarios, potentially representing a meaningful advancement in the system's ability to navigate complex driving conditions. JPMorgan also highlighted improvements in computing efficiency, which could reduce the urgency of upgrading vehicles to Tesla's next-generation AI5 hardware, although older vehicles lacking HW4 could still face limitations. The release comes as competitors including Rivian, Ford, and General Motors accelerate their own autonomous driving programs, with several targeting more advanced hands-free or eyes-off capabilities over the next two years.
